summary:
PERUSAT CREW: Operation El Niño is a cooperative educational game inspired by satellite Earth observation and flood-risk challenges in northern Peru.

Two players take complementary roles: a ground-control operator requests an observation of the Piura region, while a satellite operator plans an image capture under limited resources. Together, they transmit and assess simulated evidence, recognize the limitations of cloud-covered optical imagery, and prepare a mission report.

The prototype combines game-based learning, teamwork, and concepts from satellite operations. NASA Earth-observation resources, including GPM/IMERG, inform the scientific context, while PeruSAT-1 inspires the satellite mission scenario.

Our goal is to make space science more accessible through interactive decision-making, scientific reasoning, and responsible interpretation of evidence.
details:
PERUSAT CREW: Operation El Niño

1. The Problem

Northern Peru, especially Piura, faces serious flood risks during periods of intense rainfall. Understanding how Earth-observation missions collect, transmit, and evaluate information is important for environmental education and scientific decision-making.

Satellite science, however, can be difficult to understand without hands-on experiences.

2. Our Solution

PERUSAT CREW: Operation El Niño is a cooperative educational video game developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The project turns an Earth-observation mission into an interactive experience where two players cooperate to investigate simulated flood-risk scenarios in the Piura region.

Rather than simply displaying satellite imagery, the game teaches players to plan observations, manage resources, communicate evidence, and recognize scientific uncertainty.

3. How the Game Works

Players take two complementary roles:

Base CNOIS — Ground Control: Requests observations, selects areas of interest, evaluates received imagery, and prepares a mission report.

PeruSAT-1 — Satellite Operations: Plans observations, manages simulated energy and storage, performs image capture, and organizes data transmission.

Mission Rules

  1. Select or receive an observation request for the Piura region.
  2. Coordinate the mission between the two operators.
  3. Verify the resources required for image capture.
  4. Execute the simulated observation.
  5. Transmit the captured evidence to the ground station.
  6. Evaluate image quality and possible cloud obstruction.
  7. Submit a responsible report based on the available evidence.

Players must consider operational limitations. If clouds obstruct the optical observation, the correct scientific response is to acknowledge insufficient evidence rather than claim an unsupported conclusion.

All telemetry values, satellite operations, and mission outcomes are educational simulations.

4. Scientific Foundation and NASA Resources

The project uses NASA's Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission and its IMERG precipitation product as scientific references for understanding rainfall monitoring.

IMERG combines information from multiple satellite observations to estimate precipitation. This resource informed the environmental context and educational design of our missions.

NASA GPM / IMERG:
https://gpm.nasa.gov/data/imerg

NASA Precipitation Data Directory:
https://gpm.nasa.gov/data/directory

These resources provide scientific background. The prototype should not be interpreted as a live NASA data-processing or flood-forecasting system.

5. PeruSAT-1 and CONIDA

PeruSAT-1 and the Centro Nacional de Operaciones de Imágenes Satelitales (CNOIS) inspired the game's operational setting and the division of responsibilities between players.

The project draws on public information from Peru's space agency, CONIDA, to represent Earth-observation operations in an educational context.

CONIDA / CNOIS:
https://www.gob.pe/10396-comision-nacional-de-investigacion-y-desarrollo-aeroespacial-centro-nacional-de-operaciones-de-imagenes-satelitales

No real satellite is controlled by the game, and the project does not claim endorsement from CONIDA or NASA.

6. Technologies and Development

The project uses a web-development architecture based on:

  • React — User interface.
  • TypeScript — Game logic and typed contracts.
  • Phaser — 2D game scenes and interactions.
  • Vite — Development and application builds.
  • Zustand — Client-side state management.
  • Supabase — Architecture for multiplayer synchronization and persistence.
  • GitHub — Source control and team collaboration.
  • Vercel — Intended web deployment platform.

The prototype uses a pixel-art visual style and combines mission-planning mechanics with exploration and interactive decisions.

7. Creativity and Expected Impact

PERUSAT CREW combines cooperative gameplay with satellite mission design.

Its distinguishing features include complementary player roles, constrained resources, simulated Earth-observation operations, and evidence-based reporting.

The intended impact is educational: helping students and other players develop interest in space science, STEM, collaboration, and critical reasoning about environmental observations.

The project is not intended to replace professional disaster monitoring or emergency-response systems.

8. Use of AI / Super Intelligence

Our team used AI-assisted tools to support:

  • Brainstorming and concept development.
  • Software development, debugging, and troubleshooting.
  • Technical writing and documentation.
  • Preparation of presentation materials and pitch scripts.
  • Visual concept creation and pixel-art references.
  • Promotional video generation and editing.
  • Synthetic narration and subtitles.

Google Flow was used for AI-generated audiovisual concepts. Google Vids was used for narration and video post-production. AI-assisted coding and writing tools supported the development workflow.

AI-generated visual sequences are identified in the pitch. Such sequences illustrate the intended gameplay experience and are not presented as verified recordings of implemented features.

The original concept, engineering decisions, scientific interpretation, game design, and final submission remain the responsibility of the team.

10. Prototype Scope and Transparency

PERUSAT CREW is an educational prototype. Simulated rainfall scenarios, satellite imagery, resource values, and mission reports are not operational observations or real-time emergency forecasts.

The public repository contains the team's implementation work and development history. Features dependent on backend deployment or synchronization should be evaluated according to their actual availability in the published prototype.

Our goal is to demonstrate how cooperative game design can help communicate the scientific and engineering decisions involved in Earth-observation missions.
